card.title: Elastic modulus: Young modulus, bulk modulus, shear modulus

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: A material resists three kinds of deformation with three moduli, each stress-over-strain: **Young's modulus** $Y = FL/(A\Delta L)$ for stretching, **bulk modulus** $K = -\Delta P/(\Delta V/V)$ for uniform compression (minus sign because pressure up means volume down; compressibility = 1/K), and **shear modulus** $\eta = (F/A)/\theta$ for twisting, with the strain measured as an angle in radians.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - Y = FL/(AΔL) - K = −ΔP/(ΔV/V); compressibility = 1/K - η = F/(Aθ)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Material State Determines Available Moduli:** Solids have all three moduli ($E, B, G$). Fluids (liquids/gases) have *only* bulk modulus $B$ — they cannot sustain shear stress ($G=0$) and have no defined Young's modulus for stretching.  ·  **Isotropic Material Relations:** For isotropic solids, the three moduli are linked via Poisson's ratio $\sigma$: $E = 2G(1+\sigma) = 3B(1-2\sigma)$. These relations *do not hold* for anisotropic materials (crystals, composites) where moduli depend on direction.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Choose the modulus by the type of deformation: stretch → E, squeeze → B, twist → G.  ·  The sign in B = −P/(ΔV/V) makes the modulus positive since ΔV is negative under compression.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***Water compression*** — 0.1% squeeze needs ΔP = 2.1×10⁶ Pa ≈ 21 atm.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Covers only: elastic modulus, young modulus, bulk modulus, shear modulus (within Elasticity).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Physics — don't mix them.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Compute Young's modulus from a wire experiment data set.  ·  Compute bulk modulus from a known pressure and volume change.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "Shear strain is an angle — keep it in radians."

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Numerical (3m): A solid cube of side 20 cm is sheared by 800 N on its top face; η = 4×10¹⁰ Pa. Find θ.** — F/A = 800/0.04 = 2×10⁴ Pa; θ = 2×10⁴/4×10¹⁰ = 5×10⁻⁷ rad.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: The 2024 definition question covers bulk modulus and Poisson's ratio — know both cold.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **The minus sign in K:** pressure up → volume down; the sign makes K itself positive.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Y = FL/(AΔL); K = −ΔP/(ΔV/V); η = (F/A)/θ.  ·  Compressibility = 1/K; K_water = 2.1×10⁹ Pa.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Sound speed in a fluid is √(K/ρ) — bulk modulus sets how fast pressure waves travel.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: Young's modulus is the ratio of longitudinal stress to: → C  ·  A liquid has which elastic modulus? → C

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Three Ways to Squeeze a Solid Pull a rod, press a block, twist a shaft — three deformations, three moduli. Young's modulus answers stretching, bulk modulus answers compression, and the shear (rigidity) modulus answers twisting. Together they form the complete elastic fingerprint of a material.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Young's modulus Y (longitudinal) $$Y = \frac{\text{longitudinal stress}}{\text{longitudinal strain}} = \frac{FL}{A\,\Delta L}$$ Response to stretching/compression along one direction. Steel ≈ 2×10¹¹ Pa.…  ·  ## 3. Conceptual Relationships - **To Topic 39:** Y is one of the three moduli, all defined as stress/strain. - **To Topic 41:** σ (Poisson) connects lateral and longitudinal strains, linking Y, K, η. - **To Fluid mechanics:** K governs sound speed ($v = \sqrt{K/\rho}$ in fluids). - **To Torsion:** η governs the torsional rigidity of shafts and wires.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Geometry Separation:** $E$ is an intensive material property (Pa), while spring constant $k = EA/L$ is extensive. Changing a wire's length or cross-section changes $k$ but not $E$ — this distinction is essential for connecting spring problems to material science.  ·  **Three moduli, one idea:** each is stress ÷ strain for a different deformation type — stretch (Y), squeeze (K), twist (η).  ·  **Liquids have K only** — they resist compression but not shape change.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Convert areas to m² before computing stress (1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m², 1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m²).  ·  The relation E = 2G(1+σ) lets you compute Poisson's ratio from E and G.  ·  NEB commonly asks to compute one modulus from two others using the linking relations.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Verified PYQ: bulk modulus + Poisson's ratio definitions (2024, 3m).  ·  "Bulk modulus is the ratio of volumetric stress to volumetric strain."  ·  Why is rubber's bulk modulus high even though it deforms easily?

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Compute shear modulus from a tangential force and shear angle.  ·  Evaluate Poisson's ratio from given E and G.  ·  Compare the compressibility of steel, water, and air.
